title: Pressing-plant costs, the Cleveland shipment and independents
summary: Lee describes paying 13 cents a record, shipping 10,000 to Cleveland, and getting back mostly old records instead of sales.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Yeah. So, you know, if you don't have knowledge of something, then you suspect -- and I'd heard so many stories how they take your records and -- one of the biggest mistakes I made in my life was not taking that money! Because I put the record out myself, and they really took me pretty good, because the pressing plants get you when you're new; I had to pay 13¢ a record, and after I found about it later when I was accepted, I didn't have to pay but 9¢, you know. And you ship these records to Cleveland; to all the different places all over.

I sent 10,000 to Cleveland. This is a funny story, I think; this was when I really got my feet wet! I shipped this fellow 10,000 in Cleveland, and I kept billing him and wondering when he's gonna send me my money. So he told me, I'm gonna ship you your records back because I didn't sell but 300 and something so he paid me for 300 and something, and the records were sitting up in my office, and I said, now what I should do is take these singles and use them as demos, you know, to get somebody else to record the song. The title of the song was "It Kills Me", she was singing.
Yeah. Howlett Smith was on my publishing company -- I don't know if you know him; he's a blind pianist; do you know him? Yeah, he wrote the song.

And so I said what I should do, I said, I should use these as demos. And so I broke the box open, and I reached down and I took about 15 or 20, but after the first 3, the next 17 were, you know, Gene Autry's records, anybody's records you could think of, and I started breaking the box open, and they'd put 3 of mine on top, and everything else was old time, you know, Freddie Slack records, anything. So that was really my baptism to what the record business was all about.
Wasn't there anything you could do about that?

No, there wasn't anything I could do. That's why they tell you -- independents eat you alive in the record business; if you are a small record company. That's why Motown records, you know, this is where I work now, not only an oddity but they were very fortunate because they came along at the right time. And they were in a place where they were one of a kind, you know, Motown was the only record company in Detroit. So they had that where they could make it. But for an independent record company to make it, the distributors would eat you alive.
